content: The rapid and high increase in arterial nicotine plasma concentrations observed with cigarette smoking is not achieved with the nicotine inhaler. Following the use of a single inhaler, arterial nicotine concentrations rise gradually to an average of 6 ng/mL, in contrast to cigarette smoking, where nicotine levels increase rapidly and reach a mean peak concentration (Cmax) of approximately 49 ng/mL within 5 minutes. The release of nicotine from the inhaler is temperature-dependent, as studied in 18 patients across a temperature range of 68°F to 104°F. At ambient room temperature, the average steady-state plasma nicotine levels achieved after 20 minutes of intensive inhalation per hour are approximately 23 ng/mL. At higher temperatures of 86°F and 104°F, the corresponding plasma nicotine levels increase to approximately 30 ng/mL and 34 ng/mL, respectively. The peak plasma nicotine concentration (Cmax) at steady-state is achieved after 20 minutes of intensive inhalation per hour over a 10-hour period. When the nicotine inhaler is used ad libitum, typical plasma nicotine levels range between 6 and 8 ng/mL, which is about one-third of the levels achieved with cigarette smoking. The volume of distribution of nicotine following intravenous administration is approximately 2 to 3 L/kg. Nicotine binds to plasma proteins at a rate of less than 5%, meaning that changes in plasma protein levels due to concomitant drug use or disease states are unlikely to significantly affect nicotine kinetics. Nicotine undergoes extensive metabolism, with more than 20 metabolites identified, all of which are less active than the parent compound. The primary urinary metabolites are cotinine (15% of the dose) and trans-3-hydroxycotinine (45% of the dose). Cotinine has a half-life of 15 to 20 hours and is present in concentrations that exceed nicotine by a factor of 10. The liver is the primary site of nicotine metabolism, with the kidney and lung also contributing to its metabolism. Approximately 10% of absorbed nicotine is excreted unchanged in the urine. This percentage can increase to as much as 30% with high urine flow rates and urinary acidification below a pH of 5. The apparent elimination half-life of nicotine is 1 to 2 hours. Pharmacokinetic parameters such as area under the curve (AUC) and Cmax are approximately 40% and 30% lower, respectively, in females compared to males. However, there are no clinically significant differences in the kinetics of the nicotine inhaler between males and females. Nicotine itself does not appear to be carcinogenic in laboratory animals. However, when combined with tumor-initiating agents, nicotine and its metabolites have been shown to increase the incidence of tumors in the cheek pouches of hamsters and the forestomach of F344 rats. One study, which could not be replicated, suggested that cotinine, the primary metabolite of nicotine, may cause lymphoreticular sarcoma in the large intestine of rats. Neither nicotine nor cotinine was found to be mutagenic in the Ames Salmonella test. Nicotine induced reparable DNA damage in an E. coli test system and was shown to be genotoxic in a test system using Chinese hamster ovary cells. In rats and rabbits, nicotine has been shown to delay or inhibit implantation by reducing DNA synthesis. Studies have also demonstrated a decrease in litter size in rats treated with nicotine during gestation. The efficacy of nicotine inhaler therapy as an aid to smoking cessation was demonstrated in two single-center, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials involving a total of 445 healthy patients. The recommended treatment duration was 3 months, but patients were allowed to continue using the product for up to 6 months if desired. Quit rates, defined as the percentage of individuals who continuously abstained from smoking after week 2, were higher with the nicotine inhaler compared to placebo at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months. After using the nicotine inhaler, the mouthpiece should be carefully separated, the used cartridge removed and discarded out of the reach of children and pets, and the mouthpiece stored in the provided plastic storage case for future use. The mouthpiece is reusable and should be cleaned regularly with soap and water. Nicotine inhaler cartridges can be detected on radiograms. The product is supplied as 168 cartridges, each containing 10 mg of nicotine (4 mg delivered), along with 5 mouthpieces, 28 storage trays (each containing 6 cartridges), and 1 plastic storage case. A patient information leaflet is included in the package. The product should be stored at room temperature, not exceeding 77°F (25°C), and cartridges should be protected from light. Patients should be advised to read the information sheet carefully and consult their physician or pharmacist regarding proper use. Both used and unused cartridges must be kept out of the reach of children and pets. The interaction between alcohol and the nicotine inhaler has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor about the effects of consuming alcohol while using this medication.
